stories.headline: Denver man sentenced to 32 years in prison for girlfriend's murder
stories.summary:
Innis Lee Collins, 42, was sentenced Monday to 32 years in prison for the second-degree murder of 19-year-old Namantha Noller Rice, whose body was found in the stairwell of a Denver apartment building near East 16th Avenue and Broadway in April 2022. Collins pleaded guilty in August under a plea deal that resulted in dismissal of first-degree murder, body tampering, and evidence destruction charges.

Surveillance footage captured Collins carrying an unconscious Rice from his apartment into the stairwell, then leaving, changing clothes, and returning to the building. Collins had previously been arrested on an assault charge involving Rice in February 2022, though that case does not appear in state court records.

The case drew attention to ongoing concerns about domestic violence in Denver. Rice was 19 years old at the time of her death.

stories.headline: Denver motorcycle officer seriously injured in crash while responding to call
stories.summary:
A Denver Police Department motorcycle officer suffered serious but non-life-threatening injuries Thursday evening after a crash at West 13th Avenue and North Bannock Street. The officer had emergency lights and sirens activated and was responding to a call at the time of the collision with a motorist.

Denver police announced the incident on X at approximately 5:40 p.m. and said the department was investigating the circumstances of the crash. No further details about the motorist involved were immediately released.

The incident adds to ongoing scrutiny of traffic safety conditions for Denver officers operating in the city's busy street grid.

stories.headline: Denver police officers erroneously told residents they could not file crash reports after insurance exchange
stories.summary:
Some Denver Police Department officers incorrectly told residents that drivers who exchanged insurance information at the scene of a traffic crash had converted the incident into a civil matter, preventing officers from writing crash reports or issuing citations. The department acknowledged the error after resident John Schroyer filed complaints with his city council representative following a June 5 crash in which a driver ran a red light at Kalamath and Alameda.

Officer William Ladouceur responded to Schroyer's crash and declined to write a report or cite the at-fault driver, citing a legal prohibition that does not exist. A woman at a Denver police substation repeated the same incorrect explanation when Schroyer sought follow-up assistance.

Colorado's Department of Regulatory Agencies confirmed that police reports are not determinative of insurance fault but are one factor companies use in assigning blame. City Councilmember Kevin Flynn was contacted by Schroyer and is aware of the matter. The department has not publicly detailed what corrective steps, if any, have been taken.

stories.headline: Broncos host Rams in Sunday Night Football showdown with storylines beyond the field
stories.summary:
The Denver Broncos and Los Angeles Rams meet Sunday night at Empower Field at Mile High in a Week 3 matchup that carries significant stakes for both teams. Kickoff is set for 6:20 p.m. on NBC, with the Broncos entering as 2.5-point home underdogs according to FanDuel, and the over/under set at 44.5.

Both teams rebounded from difficult Week 1 losses with wins in Week 2, setting the stage for what analysts are calling a potential Super Bowl preview. The game also marks the first meeting between the clubs since a Christmas Day 2022 blowout loss that accelerated the Broncos' coaching change and front-office overhaul under owner Greg Penner.

The matchup carries an additional layer of intrigue given that Rams owner Stan Kroenke — who also owns the Nuggets and Avalanche — is a cousin by marriage to Broncos owner Rob Walton. The two ownership groups are expected to compete across professional sports and real estate in Denver for generations. Running back depth remains a concern for the Broncos heading into the game.

stories.headline: Avalanche forward Fedor Svechkov's lineup fit could reshape top-six forward group
stories.summary:
Acquired from Nashville in a June trade along with Zachary L'Heureux, Colorado Avalanche forward Fedor Svechkov is positioned to center the third line in the season opener against Utah on Saturday. The 23-year-old, a first-round pick in the 2021 NHL draft, has posted 12 goals and 34 points in 122 NHL games but has yet to fully unlock his offensive potential at the top level.

Coach Jared Bednar said Svechkov's development could directly affect where veteran Nazem Kadri fits in the lineup. If Svechkov proves capable at center, Kadri could move to the wing and into a top-six role — a significant shift given Kadri's value to the organization.

L'Heureux, also acquired in the Nashville deal, is expected to anchor an energy fourth line with Parker Kelly and Logan O'Connor. Bednar acknowledged the team will need to experiment with combinations early in the season before settling on the optimal configuration.

stories.headline: Rockies close out disappointing season on winning note as they face White Sox in final series
stories.summary:
The Colorado Rockies enter their final series of the 2026 season against the Chicago White Sox on a five-game losing streak, following a 12-8 loss to the Arizona Diamondbacks on Thursday in which Cole Carrigg recorded four hits. Despite the recent skid, the Rockies are projected to finish with 14 to 17 more wins than they managed in 2025, representing measurable improvement.

The Chicago series also offers the Rockies a chance to face former outfielder Brenton Doyle, who departed Colorado before this season. The final games serve as an evaluation opportunity for the organization heading into the offseason.

The series marks the end of a transitional year for the franchise as it continues its long-term rebuilding effort.

stories.headline: Denver International Airport ranks near bottom of mega airports in passenger satisfaction study
stories.summary:
Denver International Airport ranked 18th out of 20 mega airports in the 2026 North America Airport Satisfaction Study by J.D. Power, scoring 602 out of 1,000 points. Minneapolis-Saint Paul International Airport topped the rankings for the third consecutive year with a score of 684. DIA's score represents a six-point improvement over last year, with the largest gains in airport staff and ease of travel.

J.D. Power attributed DIA's low ranking in part to the ongoing $1.3 billion Great Hall renovation project, which is expected to be completed by December 2027. The study surveyed 24,710 travelers between July 2025 and July 2026 and measured satisfaction across seven categories including terminal facilities, transportation access, and food and retail options.

DIA spokesperson Christine Pomorski acknowledged passenger frustration with construction but said the airport is already seeing meaningful improvements as renovation milestones are completed. J.D. Power's managing director noted that airports typically see satisfaction rebound significantly once construction concludes.

stories.headline: Carpio-Sanguinette Park reopens after decade-long transformation from toxic industrial site to 80-acre urban park
stories.summary:
Denver has reopened Carpio-Sanguinette Park and Heron Pond Open Space in the city's Northside neighborhood after a decade of remediation and redevelopment at the site of a former wastewater treatment facility. The 80-acre complex at East 51st Avenue and Emerson Street features a BMX pump track, an elaborate nature-themed playground, paved accessible paths, and a bird blind and observation tower overlooking Heron Pond.

The pond was formerly contaminated with arsenic, cadmium, and lead. The project involved a major partnership between Denver Parks and Recreation and the Department of Transportation and Infrastructure, which used enterprise funds to address contamination damage. The park unites four formerly separate parcels into a single connected open space.

Designers preserved the site's graffiti-covered concrete infrastructure from the industrial era as public art monuments, with ongoing community permission to add to designated walls. City officials noted the project is particularly significant because Denver has almost no remaining open land available for new parks. Great blue herons, egrets, migrating ducks, and other birds regularly use the protected natural area.

stories.headline: Colorado offers $10 Uber credits to reduce drunk driving during football season
stories.summary:
The Colorado Department of Transportation is offering residents a $10 Uber rideshare credit through Oct. 16 as part of a campaign to reduce impaired driving during the early weeks of football season. The credit, available in the Uber app using a promotional code, was developed in partnership with AAA Colorado.

The initiative coincides with a heightened DUI enforcement period running from Thursday through Oct. 21, during which law enforcement agencies statewide are operating sobriety checkpoints and increased patrols. Last year, 88 people were killed in DUI-related crashes during the same period, and 1,427 DUI arrests were made in October alone.

Colorado State Patrol Chief Col. Matthew C. Packard urged residents to arrange sober transportation regardless of how much they have consumed. So far in 2026, law enforcement has made 9,322 DUI arrests statewide, with Lake, Clear Creek, and Montezuma counties recording the highest per-capita rates.

stories.headline: NTSB report: San Juan Mountains plane crash that killed two dropped 450 feet in one minute
stories.summary:
A preliminary National Transportation Safety Board report released Friday found that a single-engine Cessna T206H that crashed near Telluride on Sept. 3, killing two men, lost approximately 450 feet of altitude in one minute before striking the mountainside near Dolores Peak. The plane had taken off from Grand Junction at 1:41 p.m. and was returning to Belen, New Mexico after completing aerial survey work when the crash occurred.

The two victims were identified as pilot Randy Ramirez, 34, and camera operator Blake Klobuchar, 20, both employees of Vexell Imaging Inc. A hiker in the area reported windier-than-normal conditions at the time, with recorded wind speeds of 9 mph and gusts to 28 mph. Denver Air Traffic Control flagged the plane as missing around the same time a hiker reported seeing smoke on the north side of Dolores Peak.

Ramirez had been flying since 2016 and joined the surveying company in April. Klobuchar had worked for the company since March 2025. The NTSB will publish a final report including probable cause determinations within two years.

stories.headline: Colorado doctor raises alarm over rising kratom use among teens following student deaths
stories.summary:
A Denver-area physician is warning about increasing kratom use among teenagers in Colorado following the deaths of students at the University of Mississippi linked to the substance. Dr. Casey Wolf, interim chief medical officer at WellPower, a Denver mental health and substance abuse care center, said she has observed a rise in adolescent kratom consumption in recent years.

Kratom, derived from a Southeast Asian plant, is marketed in some circles as a natural supplement but has been associated with overdose deaths when combined with other substances. In 2021, a 33-year-old Denver man, Daniel Bregger, died from an overdose combining kratom and diphenhydramine, the active ingredient in Benadryl.

The substance is currently unregulated in Colorado and is widely available in gas stations and supplement stores. Health officials are urging parents and educators to be aware of the drug's growing presence in teen social circles.

stories.headline: Taco Bell 50K ultrarace returns to Denver metro, hitting 10 restaurants across 31 miles
stories.summary:
A distinctive 31-mile footrace requiring participants to eat fast food at 10 Denver-area Taco Bell locations is scheduled for Oct. 3, starting at 7:30 a.m. at the 447 S. Broadway location. Runners must consume specific menu items — including at least one Chalupa Supreme or Crunchwrap Supreme by the fourth stop, and a Burrito Supreme or Nachos Bell Grande by the eighth — and finish the course in under 11 hours.

The event drew more than 700 participants last year. The course record of four hours and 28 minutes was set by professional ultrarunner Sage Canaday in 2024. Use of antacid products including Pepto-Bismol, Alka-Seltzer, Pepcid AC, and Mylanta is prohibited while on course.

The race has developed a following among endurance athletes and food-challenge enthusiasts in the Denver area.

topStory.headline: Supreme Court Blocks Missouri's Redrawn Congressional Map, Orders Return to 2022 Districts for 2026 Elections
topStory.summary:
The U.S. Supreme Court unanimously ruled Friday that Missouri must use its 2022 congressional district map for the 2026 elections, striking down the Republican-drawn 2025 map that critics had labeled a partisan gerrymander. The unsigned decision declared that state law governs the matter and that the court's earlier September 10 order had already established the 2022 map as the operative boundaries for the upcoming election cycle.

The ruling concludes a three-week period of legal turbulence during which the map governing Missouri's November congressional elections changed five times, drawing repeated court intervention at the state, federal district, appellate, and Supreme Court levels. The court found that both the 8th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals and U.S. Chief District Judge Stephen Clark had misread the September 10 order when they subsequently directed use of the 2025 map, and that reinstating the newer map at this stage would create, in the court's words, 'electoral chaos.'

The 2025 map, drawn by the Republican-controlled Missouri legislature, was widely seen as targeting U.S. Rep. Emanuel Cleaver, a Kansas City Democrat, by extending his 5th Congressional District deep into rural Republican-leaning counties along the Missouri River. Under the 2022 boundaries, Cleaver won his district with 60 percent of the vote in each of the past two election cycles. The gerrymander was designed to give Republicans a better chance at capturing a seventh Missouri seat in the U.S. House.

The practical fallout of the decision is significant for local election administrators. Voters in 28 counties will find themselves in different congressional districts for November than they were during the August 4 primary, affecting the 1st, 2nd, 3rd, 4th, and 6th districts in addition to the 5th. Missouri Solicitor General Lou Capozzi, writing on behalf of Secretary of State Denny Hoskins, had argued in the state's final brief that election chaos was unavoidable regardless of the outcome, citing likely violations of federal deadlines for sending ballots to military and overseas voters.

Rep. Cleaver, in a joint fundraising appeal with 1st District Rep. Wesley Bell of St. Louis sent Friday morning before the ruling, described the prolonged litigation as 'a never-ending case of Groundhog Day.' The decision effectively closes Republican efforts to redraw Missouri's congressional map for this election cycle, though the underlying legal and legislative disputes over redistricting in the state may continue beyond 2026.
